answer.exemplar: A price is a signal and a dividend is a transfer, so paying half the revenue back does not weaken the incentive to avoid taxed fuel, it shares the proceeds, and that is why this design is called revenue recycling and why it answers the objection that a tax falls hardest on low-income households. The tariff half is where the design can fail on its own terms: an electricity price cut lowers the cost of consuming electricity, so measured use can rise and eat the expected saving, and the failure is structural rather than accidental because the instrument that funds the compensation is the same instrument that rewards using more of the good. The rest is arithmetic: only half the revenue comes back, so the other half has to buy reductions that do not themselves create demand, such as retiring inefficient plant or funding insulation, and if it is simply spent elsewhere then the tax has raised cost without buying the missing tonnes. A weak answer treats the recycling as cancelling the tax, or treats the tariff cut as free because the money came from the same bill.

questions.explanation: A strong answer separates a transfer from a price: the dividend and the tariff cut redistribute the money without weakening the price signal, so the incentive to avoid taxed fuel survives, and the distributional objection is answered rather than dismissed. It should then identify the self-defeating case, that a lower electricity price is itself an incentive to use more and so can shrink the saving it funds, and note that only half the revenue returns, so the remaining half must buy reductions that do not add demand. An answer that says the recycling cancels the tax, or that calls the tariff cut free because the money came from the same bill, has confused a transfer with a change in the price.
questions.hint: Ask whether the money comes back as a transfer or as a lower price on the thing being taxed.

answer.exemplar: The recurring round is the design's real strength: a five-year cycle turns an abstract intention into a dated, public number that an election or a budget can be held to, and a published number is something domestic actors can use against a government that would rather promise less. Its weakness is that ambition is then entirely self-assessed, and with no penalty and no review a government that promises little loses nothing, so the agreed total is the sum of choices made for domestic reasons and a target far below what a country could do looks exactly like a target at its limit. A stronger design keeps the national choice but adds three things: a common accounting rule so the same tonne is reported the same way everywhere, a duty to state a direction and a range between submission years rather than a single endpoint, and a review that compares a submitted target with the country's own enacted policy and with the pathways the physical science allows, so that an ambitious target and a lazy one can be told apart. It is worth conceding that any such comparison is itself contestable, which is why the review is better spent on consistency and transparency than on trying to assign each country its precise share.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the recurring round as the strength, because a dated public target is something domestic politics can be held to, and names self-assessment as the weakness, because with no penalty and no review a government that promises little loses nothing and a weak target cannot be told from a genuine limit. It should then specify what a stronger design adds: common accounting and reporting, an obligation to move in a stated direction between rounds rather than only at endpoints, and a review that compares a submitted target with the country's own enacted policy and with what the science allows. An answer that treats the lack of a penalty as a strength, or that proposes penalties without naming the transparency that makes a target checkable, has reversed the two roles.
questions.hint: Ask what a dated public number buys, and what happens when nobody checks it.
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a treaty built on self-declared targets with no penalty

answer.exemplar: With one price across the fleet every operator compares the price of a tonne saved against the price of a tonne emitted, so the cheapest savings move first and the target is met at the smallest total cost, which is a claim about ordering rather than about any particular technique, and the same price pays an inventor whose new burner undercuts what everyone else pays, so the incentive points at options nobody has built yet. A standard works differently: it names the performance or the technique in advance, so the regulator commits to a cost before knowing which approach exists, and if it guesses the expensive one the target is met on schedule at twice the price, as the 0.9 and 1.8 billion figures in a comparable case show. The standard's advantages are not trivial either: with few large sources and well understood engineering a definite target is easier to verify than a fuel price, and it does not depend on monitoring that a small operator cannot meet. The two failures to avoid are treating administratively simple as automatically cheap and treating a price as a guarantee of innovation, since a price only ranks the options on offer and the options are set by what exists and by what someone is willing to build.

questions.explanation: A strong answer says a uniform price equalises the cost of the last tonne saved across operators, so the cheapest cuts happen first, the total cost is the least available, and the incentive points at an option nobody has built yet, while a standard names a technique in advance and therefore commits the regulator to a cost before the options are known, with a two-fold spread available when it guesses. It should also concede that a standard has real advantages where sources are few and the engineering is well understood, because a definite target is easier to verify than a fuel price. The two beliefs to reject are that administratively simple means cheap and that a price guarantees innovation, since a price ranks the options on offer rather than choosing one.
questions.hint: Ask which instrument requires someone to name a technique before the options are known.
